name: EGF mesotherapy

lead:
EGF mesotherapy uses epidermal growth factor, a 53-amino-acid protein that promotes cell growth, delivered into or onto the skin through small injections or microneedling in aesthetic clinics. The aim is skin renewal and a smoother, firmer look.
EGF was discovered by Stanley Cohen, who shared the 1986 Nobel Prize with Rita Levi-Montalcini. Medical use is best known for the recombinant product Heberprot-P in diabetic foot ulcers.

paras: Clinics deliver EGF-containing preparations by superficial injection or needling, usually in sessions repeated over time and combined with other skin treatments. Details vary by clinic.
Safety of EGF has been described as poorly studied; the cosmetic injection use is not a regulator-approved indication.

chain: Signals cells to grow and renew
angle.text: Practitioners use it to stimulate skin renewal for a smoother, fresher look. The cosmetic claim is built on EGF's known role in cell growth.

lead: Epidermal growth factor (EGF) is a 53-amino-acid protein, about 6 kDa, that binds the EGF receptor and promotes cell growth and differentiation.[1] It occurs in platelets, saliva, tears, milk and urine.[1] Stanley Cohen found it while working with Rita Levi-Montalcini, and they shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[1]

In aesthetics, 'EGF mesotherapy' refers to delivering EGF preparations into the skin by small injections or needling, with the goal of skin rejuvenation. The medical product built on recombinant human EGF, Heberprot-P, is used for diabetic foot ulcers, where it can be injected or applied topically; evidence of improved healing is described as tentative and safety as poorly studied.[1]

paras: EGF was the second growth factor identified.[1] Human EGF was originally called urogastrone.[1]
Recombinant human EGF is sold as Heberprot-P for diabetic foot ulcers.[1]
No studies found for cosmetic EGF mesotherapy specifically. Studies of EGF in diabetic foot ulcers are a separate, wound-healing category.[1]

timeline.event: Cohen and Levi-Montalcini share the Nobel Prize for growth-factor discoveries.[1]
